elements.content: Abstract?Hallucination rates in small language models (1B to 3B parameters) remain high when performing extractive scientific synthesis. We propose a deterministic evidence verification layer that breaks generated responses into atomic factual claims and validates n-gram overlap, numerical values, and bounding-box coordinates against retrieved source passages. Empirical trials show hallucinated citations drop by 78.4% without requiring expensive model fine-tuning.

elements.content: 1. Introduction & Methodology When local open-weight models such as LLaMA-3.2 (1B/3B) or Qwen-2.5 (1.5B) run on consumer CPUs, their generation cannot be assumed mathematically sound. In high-stakes research intelligence, asserting an unverified claim can compromise scientific integrity.

elements.content: 2. Deterministic Claim Decomposition & Alignment Our verification layer operates in three discrete stages: 1. Atomic claim decomposition: Answer strings are partitioned into verifiable propositions. 2. Lexical and numeric alignment: Exact matching of reported metric percentages (e.g., 94.2%) and keyword n-grams. 3. Confidence calibration: A deterministic score between 0.0 and 1.0 is computed without LLM prompt fabrication:

elements.content: 4. Stated Limitations The authors note that purely lexical and n-gram overlap can occasionally misclassify valid high-level abstract paraphrases as partially supported rather than fully verified. A hybrid syntactic dependency parser could mitigate this in future iterations.

elements.content: 5. Conclusion Deterministic post-hoc verification provides a reliable, transparent safeguard against hallucinated citations, enabling safe deployment of lightweight local models in scientific research workflows.
